summary: Proposes a common architecture for multihoming in both mobile and fixed networks, using Mobile IP (RFC 3775) and NEMO (RFC 3963). The proposal requires modifications to existing mechanisms. It is an experimental protocol.

eli5.summary: Having two roads to the Internet means you still connect if one breaks. This note proposes using moving-network tools to manage the two roads.

subtitle: Using Mobile IP and NEMO protocols to improve network availability for small fixed networks.

tldr.problem: Small networks need redundancy and load balancing across multiple internet service providers, but conventional BGP-based multihoming solutions increase global routing table size and make load balancing difficult. Small office and home networks lack a practical way to use multiple links efficiently.
tldr.mechanism: Adapt the mobile networking protocols (Mobile IP and Network Mobility) to manage multiple connections in fixed networks. A mobile router registers multiple Care-of Addresses (CoAs) with a Home Agent, and multiple Home Agents can be distributed geographically for redundancy. The Home Agent advertises aggregated prefixes to avoid adding routing entries.
tldr.outcome: Small networks can now achieve multihoming by reusing proven mobile networking technology, avoiding the scaling problems of BGP and eliminating the need to renumber IP addresses when topology changes.

today: RFC 4908 is an Experimental protocol and remains the proposal for using Mobile IP and NEMO for fixed network multihoming. It has not become a standard, but it demonstrates a proof of concept that mobile networking protocols can effectively solve multihoming problems for small networks.

sections.title: The Problem with BGP Multihoming
sections.content:
Traditional multihoming for networks relies on the Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) to advertise network prefixes to multiple Internet Service Providers. However, this approach has two main problems. First, when multihomed networks connect to different ISPs separately (rather than through a single ISP), each must advertise its own prefix without aggregation, adding one routing entry per network to the global routing table. With many small multihomed networks, this creates explosive growth in routing table size. Second, BGP is designed for routing decisions, not traffic control: it is difficult to use BGP to manage incoming traffic load balancing.

For small networks (home offices, small businesses), the overhead and complexity of managing BGP is impractical. A simpler solution that preserves IP addresses and improves availability is needed.
sections.eli5: When many small networks try to use two internet connections, each one adds an entry to routing tables everywhere. That gets big and slow. Plus, it is hard to balance traffic fairly between the two connections.

sections.title: Mobile IP and NEMO Architecture
sections.content:
Mobile IP (RFC 3775) and Network Mobility (NEMO, RFC 3963) were designed to handle devices and networks that move and change their network attachment point. The core idea is that a mobile device or mobile network maintains a home address and a Home Agent (HA) that knows where it currently is. The device registers a Care-of Address (CoA)—its current location—with the Home Agent, which tunnels packets to it.

This RFC proposes using this same architecture for small fixed networks that want multihoming. A border router (called a mobile router in the NEMO terminology) registers multiple CoAs—one for each link to an ISP—with a Home Agent. The Home Agent advertises the network's prefix to the internet. This avoids the per-link routing entries: the Home Agent aggregates multiple prefixes under its control and advertises one aggregated prefix, keeping the global routing table small.
sections.eli5: Instead of telling the internet 'I have two cables, here are both routes', you tell one central place 'I have two cables'. That place forwards everything to you down whichever cable is best, and the internet only knows about the one place.

sections.title: Multiple Care-of Addresses and Redundancy
sections.content:
In the proposed architecture, a mobile router (MR), which is the border router of the multihomed network, establishes multiple tunnels to the Home Agent by registering multiple Care-of Addresses. If the mobile router has two ISP connections, it registers two CoAs—the IP address assigned on each ISP's link. The Home Agent maintains bindings for all CoAs.

For resilience, multiple Home Agents should be deployed across the internet. All Home Agents share the same binding information through synchronization protocols (such as the Inter Home Agent Protocol, HAHA). When multiple HAs advertise the same prefix from geographically different locations, packets are routed to the nearest Home Agent based on standard routing topology. This is the same approach used by Content Delivery Networks (CDNs). Route selection and forwarding across multiple CoAs is outside the scope of this RFC.
sections.eli5: The central place (Home Agent) needs to not be a single point of failure. So you have several copies of it, in different places, all synchronized, so if one fails the others keep working.

sections.title: Protocol Extensions Needed
sections.content:
The current Mobile IP and NEMO Basic Support protocols do not allow a single home address to be bound to more than one Care-of Address simultaneously. To support multihoming, these protocols must be extended to allow multiple CoA registrations. The RFC references work (then in progress) to define a multiple Care-of Address registration mechanism that would allow the mobile router to bind the network's home address to multiple CoAs at the same Home Agent.

Additionally, when multiple Home Agents are used, they must be able to synchronize binding information. The HAHA protocol, analogous to Internal BGP (IBGP) in routing, enables this through either full-mesh or hierarchical (route-reflector-like) topologies, allowing simplified operation by using a central synchronization point.
sections.eli5: The mobile IP system needs two upgrades: it needs to let one address point to two places at once, and the central places need to copy their knowledge to each other.

sections.title: Practical Benefits and Experimentation
sections.content:
The authors implemented and tested the proposed architecture on both private test networks and the live internet. In their experiments, a mobile router had two upstream ISP connections and two CoAs for each organization, registering all four addresses with the Home Agent using the multiple-CoA option. The system operated successfully.

Beyond immediate redundancy and load balancing, the Mobile IP and NEMO approach offers an operational benefit: when network equipment is relocated or office networks change topology, the internal IP addresses and prefixes do not need to change because they are not tied to any particular ISP's prefix. This eliminates the costly and disruptive process of renumbering addresses.
sections.eli5: They tested it and it works. Plus, you never have to change your office IP addresses just because you moved or switched internet providers.
